channel.title: pgmesa's blog
channel.description: Hi, I'm Pablo, a computer vision and machine learning engineer. I write about how the tools we use every day work inside, usually by rebuilding them.

item.title: Why I rebuilt PyTorch's core from scratch
item.description: Three projects, one question I could not answer, and how this series is organized.

item.title: What a PyTorch tensor really is
item.description: What is really in memory when you hold a tensor, why x[1:3] costs the same at any size, and what contiguous means.

item.title: What the CPU does when your code reads memory
item.description: Caches, cache lines, the prefetcher, pages and the TLB, cache sets, SIMD registers, branch prediction, cores and threads, measured with tensors. The hardware background the rest of the series refers to.

item.title: How PyTorch walks a tensor of any shape
item.description: An odometer for the indices, an inner loop the compiler can vectorize, and a single division per thread.

item.title: How PyTorch prepares the loop of every operation
item.description: Broadcasting, type promotion, an output that already exists, the order of the dimensions, merging them, and the memory a tensor shares with itself.

item.title: How a PyTorch kernel uses the vector registers of every CPU
item.description: The two lambdas of a kernel, Vectorized<T> as one register, how exp is computed eight numbers at a time, and one binary that picks SSE, AVX2 or AVX-512 when it starts.

item.title: How PyTorch sums a tensor, and splits the work between threads
item.description: A reduction as a TensorIterator whose output does not move, why the obvious sum loop is slow and wrong, the cascade sum, how parallel_for splits a range, and why sum() can change with the number of threads while sum(dim) cannot.

item.title: How PyTorch computes gradients
item.description: From micrograd to PyTorch's engine, with nodes and edges, saved tensors, a dependency count instead of a recursive sort, gradients freed as the backward advances, and the reference cycle that leaks a whole graph.

item.title: How PyTorch runs the same operations on a GPU
item.description: How an operation reaches its CUDA kernel, why launches return before the work is done, a caching allocator instead of cudaMalloc, a thread per element with a division made a multiplication, and why pinned memory and the DataLoader keep the GPU busy.
